chunks.section: Learn the Directions, Normalize the Gains: Post-Training Normalization for LoRA
chunks.text: Zailong Tian Yanzhe Chen Zhuoheng Han Affiliation: Singapore Management University National University of Singapore Peking University Houfeng Wang Affiliation: Singapore Management University National University of Singapore Peking University Lizi Liao zltian@alumni.pku.edu.cn wanghf@pku.edu.cn lzliao@smu.edu.sg

While Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enables efficient task specialization, its learned updates can compromise capabilities beyond the target task. We identify adaptation imbalance : a few singular directions dominate the trained update, leaving its performance sensitive to how gains are allocated. We argue that learning where to adapt does not ensure that adaptation gains are well balanced . This motivates LoRA-Norm , a post-training normalization method that retains learned directions while rebalancing their gains. LoRA-Norm combines spectral rebalancing, a fixed nonlinear transformation of singular values, with nuclear-norm restoration, which preserves the original total spectral mass. It requires no calibration data or additional training and introduces no inference overhead. Across two backbones and three adaptation tasks, LoRA-Norm improves average specialization and capability retention, outperforming the evaluated post-hoc spectral pruning and gradient-guided editing configurations on both measures. Stronger functional equalization brings no consistent additional gains, revealing that balancing adapter gains and equalizing their responses are distinct objectives.

“The concern is not scarcity, but uneven distribution.” — Confucius, The Analects Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) specializes pretrained models by learning compact updates while keeping the original weights frozen ( Hu et al., 2021 ; Dettmers et al., 2023 ) . However, freezing pretrained parameters does not preserve pretrained behavior: the added update can improve the target task while compromising capabilities outside the adaptation distribution ( Shuttleworth et al., 2024 ) . This creates a practical challenge for deployment, where specialization and capability retention both matter ( Biderman et al., 2024 ) . An important question is whether a completed adapter can better satisfy these objectives through changes to how its learned directions are used. We examine this question by separating an adapter’s directions from their gains, building on a broader line of parameter-efficient methods that exploit weight decomposition or directional structure ( Meng et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Lingam et al., 2024 ) . The decomposition B ​ A = U ​ diag ⁡ ( σ ) ​ V ⊤ BA=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma)V^{\top} expresses the update through learned singular directions and the strengths assigned to them. Although LoRA constrains the update rank, it does not require adaptation strength to be distributed evenly across these directions. Our measurements reveal substantial concentration in trained adapters, with directional output energy dominated by a small subset of the available components. We describe this uneven allocation as adaptation imbalance and investigate its deployment consequences by changing gains while keeping the learned directions fixed.

Our central argument is that learning where to adapt does not ensure that adaptation gains are well balanced . Training jointly determines directions and gains through a source-task objective, but the resulting configuration can remain improvable for specialization and broader capability retention. Prior work establishes the feasibility of post-training refinement through weight interpolation ( Wortsman et al., 2022 ) , spectral pruning ( Kumaravelu et al., 2026 ) , and calibration-gradient-guided reweighting ( Tian et al., 2026 ) . We investigate a simpler intervention: a fixed normalization rule that revisits the gains of a completed adapter using only its parameters. Figure 1: Learn the directions, normalize the gains. LoRA training learns useful adaptation directions, but the gains assigned to these directions can become imbalanced. LoRA-Norm keeps the learned directions fixed and rebalances only their gains after training, improving specialization while preserving capabilities beyond the target task. We propose LoRA-Norm , which combines spectral rebalancing with nuclear-norm restoration , as shown in Fig. 1 . Spectral rebalancing applies a short, fixed sequence of nonlinear transformations to the singular values while preserving their associated directions. Nuclear-norm restoration rescales the transformed gains to preserve their original sum within each module. This changes the allocation of spectral mass without requiring an exactly flat spectrum. The edited update is reconstructed as standard low-rank factors with the original adapter configuration and scaling. LoRA-Norm therefore requires no calibration data or additional training and introduces no inference overhead.

We evaluate 18 trained adapters spanning two backbones and three adaptation tasks in coding, mathematical reasoning, and instruction following. LoRA-Norm improves average target-task performance and capability retention, exceeding the evaluated spectral-pruning and gradient-guided editing configurations on both measures. These results show that the same learned directions can support better deployment performance after gain normalization, without any additional training. Our analysis also clarifies what this improvement means. Preserving nuclear norm does not preserve update magnitude, and a direction’s functional contribution depends on both its gain and the inputs that activate it ( Paischer et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) . Controls matched to LoRA-Norm’s activation-weighted update energy recover much of its benefit, while stronger functional equalization provides no consistent additional gains. Thus, balancing adapter gains and equalizing their responses are distinct objectives . Directional concentration is useful for characterizing an adapter, but uniformity alone is insufficient to judge whether an edit improves specialization and retention. In a nutshell, our contributions are summarized as follows: • Empirical insight. We characterize adaptation imbalance in trained LoRA adapters and show that their learned directions can support improved specialization and capability retention through post-training gain adjustment. • Practical method. We introduce LoRA-Norm, a fixed spectral normalization procedure that preserves learned directions and per-module nuclear mass, requiring neither calibration data nor additional training or inference operations.

• Functional analysis. We examine gain redistribution alongside update strength through matched-strength controls and activation-aware interventions, showing why stronger response equalization is not a reliable objective for adapter refinement.

LoRA learns low-rank updates while keeping pretrained weights frozen ( Hu et al., 2021 ) . PiSSA and MiLoRA initialize trainable factors from principal and minor singular components, respectively ( Meng et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) ; DoRA separates weight magnitude and direction ( Liu et al., 2024 ) ; and SCLoRA constrains singular-component growth through spectral clipping ( Wi and Park, 2026 ) . SVFT learns sparse coefficients, including off-diagonal terms, in a pretrained singular-vector basis ( Lingam et al., 2024 ) , while LoRA-XS trains a small matrix between frozen SVD-derived factors ( Bałazy et al., 2024 ) . These methods change adaptation during training. Spectral analyses also study how update strength relates to intruder directions in merged weights ( Shuttleworth et al., 2024 ; Xie and Alanwar, 2026 ) . LoRA-Norm instead revisits gains in a completed adapter’s learned basis, without further optimization.

WiSE-FT interpolates pretrained and fine-tuned weights to improve robustness ( Wortsman et al., 2022 ) , corresponding to scaling a LoRA update. Spectral Unforgetting applies hard singular-value thresholding through DG-Hard ( Abro and Tahir, 2026 ) ; SLoRA filters updates by subspace similarity to the base model ( Yang et al., 2026 ) ; and PARA uses a global singular-value threshold for nonuniform rank compression ( Kumaravelu et al., 2026 ) . Safety-oriented methods include S3LoRA, which uses spectral sharpness to guide post-hoc pruning ( Ao and Rumchurn, 2025 ) , and CSULoRA, which smoothly attenuates update components relative to an estimated safety-aligned subspace ( Marchenko Breneur et al., 2026 ) . Spectral Surgery uses calibration gradients to reweight gains while fixing singular directions, with nuclear-mass restoration ( Tian et al., 2026 ) . LoRA-Norm builds on this fixed-direction formulation, replacing gradient-guided reweighting with a fixed data-free map and studying capability retention and matched-strength controls. LoRA-Norm applies a finite nonlinear transformation with per-module nuclear-norm restoration. Scalar and exact-flattening controls test the roles of update strength and spectral shape.

Parameter spectra alone do not describe how strongly learned directions respond to inputs. EVA uses activation SVD for LoRA initialization and rank allocation ( Paischer et al., 2025 ) , while CorDA uses input covariance to guide decomposition toward task learning or knowledge preservation ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . We use activation statistics retrospectively to characterize completed adapters and construct gain controls. Our functional participation ratio applies the standard participation-ratio form for effective dimensionality ( Recanatesi et al., 2022 ) to activation-weighted directional energy; it is neither a new mathematical definition nor a direct optimization objective. The main LoRA-Norm edit remains calibration-free.

A trained LoRA adapter specifies both a set of update directions and the gains assigned to them. We investigate whether these gains can be improved after training, without relearning the directions. LoRA-Norm applies a fixed spectral transformation to an existing adapter, preserving its source singular directions and per-module nuclear norm. The editing operation requires neither training data nor gradients; activation statistics are used separately for analysis. Figure 2 provides an overview of the post-training normalization procedure. Figure 2: Overview of LoRA-Norm. A LoRA adapter learns both singular directions and their gains. LoRA-Norm keeps the learned directions fixed and applies a post-training spectral transformation to rebalance their gains, followed by nuclear-norm restoration. The resulting adapter uses the same learned directions with rebalanced gains, requiring no additional training or calibration data.

We study Qwen3-8B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) , each adapted on three primary tasks: Magicoder ( Wei et al., 2024 ) , MetaMath ( Yu et al., 2024 ) , and Tulu-3 Personas-IF ( Lambert et al., 2024 ) , the 29,980-example synthetic instruction-following subset of Tulu 3 (abbreviated Tulu). For each model–task pair, we evaluate three training runs (labeled 42, 43, and 44), yielding 18 source checkpoints. All adapters have rank 16, LoRA alpha 32, and scaling c = 2 c=2 , and target the query, key, value, output, gate, up, and down projections. Comparisons pair edits of the same source checkpoint without retraining. LoRA-Norm uses the same HNS 4 + 1 4+1 configuration on all adapter modules at full editing strength in the main comparisons; the separate sensitivity study varies only the iteration counts.

The target benchmarks for Magicoder, MetaMath, and Tulu are HumanEval (164 problems; greedy pass@1) ( Chen et al., 2021 ) , GSM8K (1,319 problems; strict accuracy) ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , and IFEval (541 prompts; prompt-level strict accuracy) ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) , respectively. We additionally evaluate Commonsense-8, the equal-weight macro accuracy over ARC-Challenge and ARC-Easy ( Clark et al., 2018 ) , BoolQ ( Clark et al., 2019 ) , HellaSwag ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) , OpenBookQA ( Mihaylov et al., 2018 ) , PIQA ( Bisk et al., 2020 ) , Social IQa ( Sap et al., 2019 ) , and WinoGrande ( Sakaguchi et al., 2020 ) , totaling 22,419 examples. Commonsense-8 serves as a retention-only category in the primary 18-checkpoint evaluation. Every adapter is evaluated on all four categories using shared benchmark-specific chat templates, parsers, and scoring code. Decoding is greedy with generation seed 42. Appendix B provides protocol details and token budgets.

For each model–task pair, we collect activations from the frozen base model on 256 fixed source-task training examples, truncated to 512 tokens, using all non-padding tokens. The three runs share the same input examples. For each source checkpoint, all edited variants reuse the activation statistics projected onto its source singular basis. These data are used only for diagnostics and activation-aware controls; LoRA-Norm itself is data-free.

We report means and sample standard deviations over three training runs per model–task pair. Overall results average all 18 source checkpoints equally. Unless otherwise specified, 95% paired intervals use 2,000 source-checkpoint bootstrap resamples on fixed test sets, keeping all method variants of each checkpoint paired. Appendix B documents training configurations and differences; Appendices C and E provide run-level results and statistical procedures.

chunks.section: Frobenius matching leaves a performance gap.
chunks.text: LoRA-Norm exceeds Scalar-F by 1.44 Target points (95% paired interval [ 0.35 , 2.44 ] [0.35,2.44] ) and 1.23 Off points ( [ 0.56 , 1.91 ] [0.56,1.91] ), while reducing FG by 0.77 points. This Frobenius-matching rule does not fully reproduce its average gains. However, Scalar-F’s module-level functional energy relative to LoRA-Norm has median 2.88: equal Frobenius norms do not imply equal functional strength.

chunks.section: Energy matching reproduces much of the benefit.
chunks.text: Scalar-E achieves similar aggregate performance (Figure 4 ). The LoRA-Norm-minus-Scalar-E differences are − 0.62 -0.62 Target points ( [ − 1.64 , 0.25 ] [-1.64,0.25] ) and + 0.32 +0.32 Off points ( [ − 0.13 , 0.83 ] [-0.13,0.83] ); neither interval excludes zero. LoRA-Norm has 0.18 points lower FG ( [ 0.04 , 0.35 ] [0.04,0.35] ). Relative to Flat-E, it gains 0.23 Off points ( [ 0.10 , 0.36 ] [0.10,0.36] ), while the Target difference is − 0.19 -0.19 ( [ − 0.62 , 0.26 ] [-0.62,0.26] ). These are metric-specific differences, not evidence of uniform superiority or equivalence. Crucially, Scalar-E gains 4.70 Target and 2.92 Off points over LoRA while leaving every module’s FPR unchanged. An increase in FPR is therefore not necessary for improvement under these interventions.

chunks.section: Exact parameter flattening is also competitive.
chunks.text: In a separate evaluation block, Flat-Nuclear preserves each module’s nuclear mass and makes its gains equal across the learned singular directions. It improves Target on 16 of 18 checkpoints and trails LoRA-Norm by only 0.15 points on average, with paired wins/ties/losses of 8/4/6 against LoRA-Norm. This limits claims that the finite-step HNS map is essential. Appendix B.3 retains that block’s own references, Flat-Fro results, and the DG-Hard identity case; its scores are not mixed with the current protocol. The controls show that functional strength must be considered when interpreting the gains. They do not establish a general shape advantage beyond energy matching. Matching holds under the fixed input statistics of Eq. ( 4 ), so it does not provide a causal decomposition of end-to-end performance. An archived Qwen–MetaMath recheck does not establish HNS superiority over calibration-selected global scaling ( + 0.39 +0.39 strict points, 95% interval [ − 1.56 , 2.34 ] [-1.56,2.34] ; Appendix H ).

chunks.section: Stronger equalization does not consistently help.
chunks.text: Partial weighting ( α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 ) raises mean FPR to 12.73, with only a 0.025-point Target gain and a 0.21-point Off decrease relative to LoRA-Norm. Full weighting and protected flattening raise FPR to approximately 16 but lower both mean Target and Off (Figure 5 ). Mean FG decreases slightly under all three interventions, so the changes are metric-dependent. Across the 54 checkpoint–intervention comparisons, higher FPR accompanies worse Target performance in 22 cases and worse Off performance in 37. Responses also differ by task: full weighting helps Llama–MetaMath but harms Qwen–Magicoder (Appendix C ). These interventions change energy as well, so they test the usefulness of pursuing stronger equalization without isolating its causal effect on target-task performance and broader capability retention.

chunks.section: FPR adds no stable predictive benefit beyond energy.
chunks.text: Within-checkpoint centered regressions with leave-one-checkpoint-out evaluation yield the same caution. Among edited variants, adding FPR to log functional-energy ratio changes held-out R 2 R^{2} by 0.0155 on Target and 0.0092 on Off, with both 95% intervals crossing zero. Within the energy-matched cohort, the changes are − 0.0767 -0.0767 and − 0.0319 -0.0319 ; full-moment PR also fails to give a stable improvement. This is a conditional analysis of relative performance within a checkpoint, using its outcome mean to define the centered target, not label-free prediction of absolute performance. Appendix E.2 gives cohorts, fitting procedures, and uncertainty estimates; Figure 6 visualizes the incremental prediction results. FPR describes how the update is redistributed across the learned singular directions, but these interventions and predictive analyses do not support maximizing it as a performance objective.

Our results show that the same learned adaptation directions can support better specialization and capability retention after gain adjustment. LoRA-Norm revisits this allocation through fixed spectral rebalancing and per-module nuclear-norm restoration, without calibration data, retraining, or inference overhead. Across 18 adapters spanning two backbones and three tasks, it improves both objectives on average. Energy-matched controls recover much of the benefit, while stronger functional equalization yields no consistent further gains, limiting claims of an independent spectral-shape advantage. Thus, balancing adapter gains and equalizing functional responses are distinct objectives. Broader model and task coverage and further controlled replications would help assess generality.

The extension evaluates three ϵ \epsilon -PARA configurations and one Spectral Surgery configuration on all 18 original source checkpoints, retaining all three existing training runs. No source adapter is retrained. Current Base, LoRA, and HNS 4 + 1 4+1 references are used rather than importing scores from the earlier Spectral Surgery paper. Table 2 reports every PARA configuration, without selecting one by test-set performance. Paired intervals use 2,000 source-checkpoint bootstrap draws on the fixed test set (Table 33 ). These describe paired run heterogeneity, not independent same-recipe training repetitions; the intervals are unadjusted for multiple comparisons. PARA is implemented through compact QR/SVD; no official implementation was available at the time of this reproduction. Zero-rank modules are excluded from the PEFT configuration, and rank/alpha patterns retain the original scaling. PARA pools singular values across adapter modules and applies a global threshold ( Kumaravelu et al., 2026 ) . With pooled singular values { σ m ​ i } \{\sigma_{mi}\} , the retained squared spectral mass satisfies ∑ m , i σ m ​ i 2 𝟏 [ σ m ​ i ≥ τ ] ∑ m , i σ m ​ i 2 ≥ ϵ , ϵ ∈ { 0.90 , 0.95 , 0.99 } . \frac{\sum_{m,i}\sigma_{mi}^{2}\mathbf{1}[\sigma_{mi}\geq\tau]}{\sum_{m,i}\sigma_{mi}^{2}}\geq\epsilon,\qquad\epsilon\in\{0.90,0.95,0.99\}. (25)

The remaining gains are unchanged, without subsequent nuclear- or Frobenius-norm restoration. Original LoRA scaling is retained; it is c = 2 c=2 across the source modules in this cohort, so including it would not change the global ordering or energy ratios. Actual retained energy meets each requested budget. Mean parameter retention is 38.16%, 54.28%, and 80.16%, respectively. Parameter retention weights a retained rank in module m m by d in , m + d out , m d_{\mathrm{in},m}+d_{\mathrm{out},m} , rather than treating ranks in differently sized modules as equal parameter costs. Spectral Surgery estimates gradient-based sensitivity from 128 training examples with calibration seed 42 ( Tian et al., 2026 ) . Calibration provenance, file hashes, and per-checkpoint timing are recorded with the experiment artifacts. It is a calibration-dependent comparator; the main LoRA-Norm edit requires neither these samples nor gradients. The comparison concerns the evaluated complete configurations and is not a controlled ablation of the gradient signal alone. The fixed publication configuration is grad_direction_residual_l1_calib128 , chosen before evaluation from the principal guided-versus-random comparison and matching repository configuration. It uses answer-only teacher-forced loss, mean-absolute normalization, asymmetric multiplicative step sizes η suppress = 2.0 \eta_{\mathrm{suppress}}=2.0 and η enhance = 0.2 \eta_{\mathrm{enhance}}=0.2 , and nuclear-norm preservation. Editing is restricted to o_proj and down_proj in every layer, whereas HNS edits all seven module families; the measured difference therefore cannot be attributed to gradient guidance alone.

The PARA stage completed 224/224 scheduled cells in 1:43:31 (job 1077); the Spectral Surgery stage completed 80/80 in 0:54:53 (job 1078), starting only after successful completion of the PARA job. These stage counts include their scheduled reference cells and must not be added to the earlier primary count as though all were new unique evaluations. At most two B300 GPUs were used concurrently. Recomputed hashes of all 18 original checkpoint weights and configurations were unchanged. The execution audit reports 12 passing implementation tests, together with successful syntax, compilation, and diff checks. An initial numerical precheck stopped before evaluation because its FP32 reconstruction error of 1.202 × 10 − 5 1.202\times 10^{-5} exceeded the initial 10 − 5 10^{-5} tolerance. After the discrepancy was attributed to rounding, the tolerance was changed to 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} ; the measured error was retained in the audit. This threshold change is reported explicitly and does not establish end-to-end prediction equivalence by itself. Across the Spectral Surgery runs, the recorded calibration-gradient time totals 487.5 seconds and the reported complete editing time totals 1061.2 seconds. The latter is the end-to-end editing time, including gradient calculation, so these totals are not added together. Mean gradient and end-to-end editing times are 27.1 and 59.0 seconds per checkpoint, respectively. No relative editing speedup is claimed without comparable LoRA-Norm timings. Whole-job durations above include evaluation and are not editing-only costs.

PARA addresses compression as well as prediction, so its parameter savings must accompany the performance comparison. Spectral Surgery’s aggregate Target gain with an Off decrease describes this evaluated configuration, rather than a necessary property of all gradient-guided edits. Neither comparison isolates functional energy from spectral shape; the controls in Section 5.2 remain necessary for interpreting that distinction. The experiment result directory is: reports/posthoc_baselines_para_spectral_surgery/ Its report.md , final_validation.json , and scheduler_jobs.tsv record the summary, integrity checks, and scheduling. The method subdirectories para/ and spectral_surgery/ contain checkpoint_results.tsv and stage reports.

A label such as 4 + 1 4+1 denotes four fast steps followed by one stable step, not an adapter rank. Every nonzero setting edits all LoRA modules at strength 1, retains rank 16 and the original adapter scaling, and restores each module’s nuclear norm. Both 4 + 1 4+1 and 8 + 2 8+2 were rebuilt and evaluated with the other variants. Only target-task performance is evaluated: HumanEval (164 problems), GSM8K (1,319 problems), and IFEval (541 prompts), respectively. Identical adapters produced identical sequences across three fresh processes on a 32-question diagnostic enriched with previously changed outputs. Alternative factorizations nevertheless changed some sequences. Zero rebuild shifts strict accuracy by − 0.59 -0.59 points on the 512-question subset: repeatability does not establish representation invariance, and this shift is not a universal noise floor. Earlier evaluations already used all 1,319 GSM8K test questions. This is an exploratory one-source target-task recheck, not independent downstream confirmation or a clean held-out selection study. It does not establish retention benefits or superiority over independently validated scaling.
